segments.text: - Hello everyone.
Welcome back to "Altium Academy".
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today, we're gonna be talking about
something I see a lot

in the one minute design
review submissions
on the "Altium Academy" channel,
and that is the use
of the signal-ground-power-signal stackup.

Now, I feel like everywhere
out there in the wild,
whether it's on LinkedIn,

or whether it's in the one
minute design review submissions,
we continue to see this stackup used

as the default stackup
for four layer PCBs.
Sometimes it's a great option,
sometimes it's not the best option.
So what I'm going to do in this video
is show you the right way to use
a signal-ground-power-signal stack up.
We're gonna hop into Altium,

take a look at some examples
and let's get started.
(upbeat music)

Now in this video we're
gonna be talking about

the right way to use a
signal-ground-power-signal stackup.
And I think the first thing to understand
is why we would typically use
a signal-ground-power-signal stackup.
There's also a variant of this,
which I've discussed in another video

that you can find linked
in the description,

which is the
signal-ground-power-ground stack up.
They're essentially the same thing.

One of the reasons that
we use a power plane
in a four layer board
is because we might need to supply
high current in the design,

and of course we may have a
digital section in the design,

and that digital section might
not have very high IO count
so you can fit everything onto one layer.
But then,
you might also need to supply high power,
and that's where the power plane comes in.
You get access to a lot of copper,
it has high current carrying capacity,

and you can deliver a lot
of power through that board.

Now, this is typical in a
digitally controlled power system,

and I've built several
of these in the past,

and that's I think the
most important instance

where you would use a power
plane in a four layer board.
But what is a more common reason

that you might use a power
layer in a four layer board

and then create the
signal-ground-power-signal stack up?

Well, one of those examples
is shown here on screen.

Here on screen I have a
four layer board pulled up

and you can see here as I
scan through the layers,

one of the reasons that
we might want to use
a dedicated power layer on layer three.

Here we have a lot of
signals and components
on the top layer.
And then when we go to layer two,
we have ground.
Here on layer three,
you can see the main reason
that we would use a dedicated power layer,

it's because we have a ton
of different power rails.
So, as I move through here,

you can start to see what
those power rails look like.
They go to a lot of different components

and they're all operating
at different voltages

or they need to be
separated from each other
for some reason.
That is one of the biggest reasons
that you would use a dedicated power layer
in a four layer board.
Then, on the fourth layer,
you can fill it with ground
to provide some additional shielding,

especially if those power
rails are quite noisy.

Or you can put signals
on that fourth layer

and then I'll show you
later in some examples
how we would handle those signals

to ensure that they have a
consistent ground reference.
So, that covers the two main reasons
that we would use a dedicated power layer
in a four layer board.
One of them is delivering high current.

The other is because we just
have a lot of voltage rails

and we just can't fit them
on the surface layers.
So, how do we deal with this
when we have a lot of voltage rails
and we want to route signals on layer four

but we don't wanna have
issues with radiated emissions

and we don't want to have
issues with EMI susceptibility?

Well, let's take a look
at a couple of examples

and we can see the right
way to handle this.
So, the first one that I wanna look at

is one of our older
design review submissions
from Neha Patil,

and this is one of the better
ones that we saw come in
and I really like this

because it did illustrate
the right way to use

a four layer board with
a dedicated power layer.

So, here in this design you
can see it is a digital design.
This is a direct digital synthesis board,

and you can see here we
have the DDS chip right here
in the center of the board.
We also have a level shifter,
and then we have quite a few power rails
that are routed on the top layer.
Now, these power rails,
they don't have to go too far,
they don't have to carry a ton of power.

So you can see for these
particular power rails shown
in frame on screen in Altium
that they can be routed on the top layer.

But if you look here in
the internal third layer,
we have two larger rails
that are both being used for power.
So, one of these is a 3.3 volt net,

and then the other one over
here is a 1.8 volt net.

So these are two VDD nets
at different voltages.

And again, this illustrates
the second reason

why we might want to use
a dedicated power layer
in a four layer board.

These two rails might need
to handle a lot of power.

They also might need to
take up a lot of space

because they need to
reach a lot of components
and so we just can't fit them
on the top layer or on the bottom layer,

it makes sense to put
them on their own layer
in the interior of the stackup.
And this is the exact same justification
that we would use in a six layer board
that has a dedicated power layer.
Now, how do we handle the signals

that might need to be
routed around on layer four?
Well, you can see here on layer four,
we do have signals in this design

and we actually have a
microcontroller on the bottom layer.

Now, we've done two things
in this design to ensure

that we can put these
signals on this bottom layer
and have low risk of radiated emissions
and low risk of susceptibility.
If I just turn off the two outer layers
on the top half of the board

and then we turn on just this
power layer on layer three,
you can see here how this routing was done

in order to ensure that we
have low rated emissions
and then we have good signal integrity.

If I look around at these
traces coming off the MCU,
you can see that they are routed

over a solid region of
copper on layer three.
So, right here,

these green lines illustrate
the splits in the power layer

that delineate between our 3V3
rail and our 1.8 volt rail.

Now you can see here
that none of the signals

in this design on layer four
are routing over the split

between the 3.3 volt rail
and the 1.8 volt rail.
Now we do have a couple of components
for this reference clock

that do get pretty close to
that edge of this 3.3 volt rail.
And I think the ideal thing to do would be
to just pick these components up
and move them down just a little bit

so that they're a little bit
farther away from that split.
But aside from that,
I like this placement and routing

because it doesn't cross
over any of the splits
between these two regions.
Now, you can see here

we have a couple of traces
over the 1.8 volt rail

and they are confined
just to the 1.8 volt rail.
So, that's really important.

These traces also don't
cross over the split.
They in fact end up over on the top layer
and once they reach the top layer,

they're then routed into the
DDS and into the level shifter.

So, this illustrates the
first piece of guidance
with working with a four layer stack up
that has a dedicated power layer.

So, that's our signal ground
power signal stack up.
If you are routing above that power layer,

you have to make sure that
you don't have any signals
crossing the gaps between your power rails
that ensures that you have low risk
of radiated emissions and susceptibility.

But there's one other
thing that we have to do
on that signal layer.
Here inside Altium,
you can see on layer four,
if I just isolate this layer,

that we have a polygon
connected to the ground net.

That polygon fills in
everywhere in this design
and it is connected to the ground net.

So, it provides a ground
reference for these signals
as they're routed through this board.

The final thing that we
need to do in this design

in order to ensure that
our ground on layer two

and our ground fill on layer
four are connected together

is to of course use stitching
vias as you can see here.
So, here there is a stitching via array
that's been automatically filled in

using the ground stitching
via tool inside Altium

that ensures that these
vias have the connection

between the top side and the
bottom side and inner grounds.

And then we have a low
impedance return path

from any ground layer to
any other ground layer.

Now, the one other thing I
wanna point out here of course,
is balancing the copper in this stack up.

And if we just go over
to the View Configuration
and we turn on the Top Layer,
you'll see what I mean.
Because we have shown

that we need to pour the
copper pour on layer four,

we also need to have
copper pour on layer one
in order to balance the stackup

and that's exactly what's
been done in this design.

So, we need to make sure
that stackup is balanced
with a symmetric copper distribution
in order to help prevent warpage.
Now, I want to make a note here.

Pouring copper on all of your
internal and external layers

is not required to
prevent warpage in the PCB
when the stackup is fabricated.
What is required is ensuring symmetry
in the copper distribution.
Basically, we would wanna make sure
that the top half copper distribution

roughly mirrors the bottom
half copper distribution.

And that's what we've done
in this four layer board
by pouring the bottom ground
and the top ground with copper pour.
Now, let's take a look at another example
from one of the recent projects
that I presented on the channel,
and that is for our NFC Reader Project.

Here I have the PCB doc file
pulled up for the NFC reader.
And if I go to the top layer,

here you can see what
this design looks like.

Basically here we have top
layer being for our components.
We have a ground layer on layer two,

and then layer three is
a bunch of power rails,

and then layer four is for
some signals as well as ground.

So, let's take a little bit of
a deeper look at this design.

And I covered some of the
points in the project video
that is linked in the description,
so make sure to go watch that video.

What I wanna do again is focus
on layer three and layer four
because we have our power on layer three
and then you can see here we also
have some routing on layer four.

Let's go ahead and
unisolate the two layers,
and here we'll just kind of turn off

some of the mechanical
and component layers
and we can see a little bit better
what this routing looks like.
We have some signals that are routed

between our microcontroller
and our RF transceiver,
and for the most part,
these signals that are being routed
between these two components
are all being routed over a solid piece
of copper on layer three.
Now, there are a few exceptions.

We have one of those
exceptions right here.
This is an LED line.
So, you can see this line is basically
just supplying power to an LED.
It's not gonna be switching repeatedly,
it's not sending data,

so we have basically no radiated
emissions from this line.
What about these other lines over here

that are routing up to the
northeast corner of the board?
Well, here you can see if we just zoom in
that some of these lines are basically
for detecting a switch.

So, these lines are
basically operating at DC.

They also don't have any
risk of radiated emissions.
They're also driving a high resistance.

So, because they're
driving a high resistance,
they will switch slowly.

So, when the microcontroller
does switch them,
they'll turn on slowly,

we don't really have any
risk of radiated emissions.
We might wanna space out
these traces right here in this region
because as you can see,
we're not getting that ground fill
in between all these traces,

but I think it's pretty low
risk for this particular design,
especially because we're using
thinner dielectrics on the outer layer.

And finally, just like we
had in Neha Patil's design,

because we have some
pour on the bottom layer

that is filling in all
of the gaps with copper,
we also want to make sure that we balance
that copper distribution in the stack up.
So, what do we need to do?

Well, then we should
also have the copper pour
on the top layer,
and that's exactly what you see here.
So, we have everything on the top layer
filled in with copper.
So, that ensures also that the signals
on the top layer and the bottom layer
have a consistent ground reference.
And of course,
we do have that ground plan on layer two

that then helps ensure that
these faster digital signals

as well as some of these
power signals on the top layer
also have a nearby ground reference

and then they have low
risk of radiated emissions.
Now so far we've looked at some examples
that show why you would use a power layer
in a four layer stack up,
and the right way to handle the routing
over that power layer.
But are there some designs
that should never use a power layer
in a four layer stack up?
Well, I think there are,

and I've pulled up one
example here inside Altium.

Now, this was also one
of these submissions
to our one minute design review series,

and this submission came
from Mohammedali Nekoui.

And if I just turn off
the component layers
and we zoom in on some of the routing,
you can start to see why we should avoid

the use of power rails
on a dedicated layer
in this particular design.
These traces have pretty high density,
and you can see here that as we zoom

into some of these regions where
the traces on the top layer

and the bottom layer
cross over each other,

we are trying to maintain an
orthogonal routing strategy
but it is pretty difficult in this design.

You do have some areas
where the traces run

parallel to each other
creating risk of crosstalk.
You also see a lot of areas in this design

where you basically
have no ground coverage
for a lot of these signals.

So, if any of these traces
are carrying digital signals

that are switching at
any appreciable rate,

they will create a lot
of radiated emissions.
Radiated emissions are reciprocal,
and if you have high radiated emissions,
you can also have high EMI susceptibility.

And that's exactly what we
would expect in the board
as it's constructed now.
Now, one thing that you can see
from the way this design has been routed
is that the power rails
are able to fit on the surface layers.

So again, this is only a
two layer board right now,

but you can see here
that we have power rails
that are routed around on this top layer.
We also have some power rails

that are routed around on
the bottom layer as well.

We can fit the power rails
on the top and bottom layer.

We don't really need to
have a dedicated power layer
in this particular design.
And because of the density of components
and the number of power rails,
I would say it would be best
to have this on a four layer board
with two internal ground planes.

That's going to ensure that
these traces on the top side
and the bottom side
are sufficiently shielded from each other.
It's going to help ensure
that they have low radiated emissions
as well as low EMI susceptibility,

and it's not going to
affect the power planes
negatively at all.
In fact, all of these power rails
are going to have much more capacitance
back to that ground layer.
Whereas here they really don't have any
capacitance to any ground layer.

And so any noise that's on
these power rails currently

could start radiating and
contribute to radiated emissions.

But if we add in some ground
with two ground layers,
we can then also reduce

the radiated emissions
from the power circuits.
So, all the way around,
this board is going to operate better
if we have it on four layers
with two internal ground planes,

particularly from the
signal integrity perspective
and EMI/EMC perspective.
Now, I'm sure I'm going to continue

to see one minute design
review submissions
and posts on LinkedIn
where people are continuing to use
the signal-ground-power-signal stackup.
And if you use it correctly,
your design can still operate successfully
and meet EMI/EMC requirements.
So, what do you think about this stackup?
Let me know in the comments.
Let me know whether you use it.
Let me know experience you have
with signal integrity and EMI/EMC.
I would love to hear from you
both here on YouTube and on LinkedIn.
Thanks for watching this video, everybody.
Make sure to hit that like button,
hit the subscribe button,

leave your comments and questions
in the comments section.
And last but not least,

don't forget to call
your fabricator folks.
We'll see you next time.
(upbeat music)

title: The Right Way to Use SIG/GND/PWR/SIG Stackups
